title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 17–18 (Night 229, continuing nights-228), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 229 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. In the fire-worshippers' underground chamber al-Asʿad remembers his brother and the glory he has lost, yearns, weeps and moans, and recites a long lament to Time: his loved ones scattered, his enemies gloating, a narrow prison with no companion but the biting of his own hand, and no friend to visit and pity him. He ends by turning his cell into a grim drinking-party — the bugs and the flea drink his blood like wine from a cupbearer's hand, the lice devour his body like a godless judge devouring an orphan's estate, he lives in a grave three cubits long, and his tears are his wine, his fetter his musician. The story then turns to his brother al-Amjad, who has waited until noon; when al-Asʿad does not come back his heart pounds, the pain of parting presses on him and his tears flow — and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-ninth night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula: the unit, al-tāsiʿatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, all in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْأَسْعَدَ تَذَكَّرَ أَخَاهُ وَالْعِزَّ الَّذِي كَانَ فِيهِ فَحَنَّ وَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَسَكَبَ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-Asʿada tadhakkara akhāhu wa-al-ʿizza alladhī kāna fīhi fa-ḥanna wa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-sakaba al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that al-Asʿad remembered his-brother and-the-might which he-was in-it; and-he-yearned and-wept, and-moaned and-complained, and-poured-out the-tears, and-recited these verses:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that al-Asʿad thought of his brother and of the glory he had once known, and he yearned and wept, moaned and lamented, and shed tears, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: The night opens by retelling the last words of the night before. The verbs then come in rhyming pairs: ḥanna / anna, “he yearned / he moaned”, and bakā / ishtakā, “he wept / he complained”. ḥanna, from the doubled root ḥ-n-n, “to long, yearn”, is said first of a she-camel crying for her home and young. anna, from the doubled root ʾ-n-n, “to moan, groan”, imperfect yaʾinnu: written وانّ, it looks exactly like the particle anna, “that”, and only the sense tells them apart. ishtakā, Form VIII of sh-k-w, “to complain”. sakaba al-ʿabarāt, “to pour out the tears”: ʿabarāt, plural of ʿabra, “a tear”. The shadda of تذكّر, العزّ, فحنّ and وانّ is printed.

sentences.t:
يَا دَهْرُ مَهْلًا كَمْ تَجُوْرُ وَتَعْتَدِي * وَلَكَمْ بِاِخْوَانِي تَرُوْحُ وَتَغْتَدِي
مَا اٰنَ اَنْ تَرْثِى لِطُوْلِ تَشَتُّتِي * وَتُرِقَّ يَا مَنْ قَلْبُهُ كَالْجَلْمَدِ
وَاَسَاْتْ اَحْبَابِيْ بِمَا اَشْمَتَ بِي * كُلُّ الْعِدَاةِ بِمَا صَنَعْتَ مِنَ الرَّدِيْ
وَقَدِ اشْتَفَى قَلْبُ الْعَدُوِّ بِمَا رَاى * مِنْ غُرْبَتِي وَصَبَابَتِي وَتَوَحُّدِي
sentences.tr:
yā dahru mahlan kam tajūru wa-taʿtadī * wa-la-kam bi-ikhwānī tarūḥu wa-taghtadī
mā āna an tarthī li-ṭūli tashattutī * wa-turiqqa yā man qalbuhu ka-al-jalmadī
wa-asaʾta aḥbābī bi-mā ashmata bī * kullu al-ʿidāti bi-mā ṣanaʿta mina al-radī
wa-qadi ishtafā qalbu al-ʿaduwwi bi-mā raʾā * min ghurbatī wa-ṣabābatī wa-tawaḥḥudī
sentences.l:
O Time, gently! How-much you-tyrannise and-transgress, * and-how-often with-my-brothers you-go-at-evening and-go-at-morning!
Has-not come-(the)-time that you-pity for-(the)-length (of) my-scattering, * and-soften, O (you) whose heart (is) like-the-rock?
And-you-have-done-ill-to my-loved-ones, by-what made-gloat over-me * all the-enemies, by-what you-did of the-evil.
And-already has-been-healed (the) heart (of) the-enemy by-what it-saw * of my-exile and-my-love-longing and-my-solitude.
sentences.i:
O Time, go gently! How you oppress me and wrong me, * how often you carry off my brothers, at nightfall and at dawn!
Has the time not come for you to pity me, so long cast adrift, * and to relent, you whose heart is like a rock?
You have done my loved ones harm, and all my enemies * gloat over me for the evil you have worked.
The enemy's heart has had its fill of what it saw * of my exile, my longing and my loneliness.
sentences.n: The first four lines of a poem of seventeen in the metre kāmil, all on one rhyme, -dī; the short final -i of the rhyme word is sung long. The print points the verse fully. yā dahru, “O Time”: dahr is time as fate, the destroyer, the old target of complaint in Arabic verse. mahlan, “gently!”, an accusative standing for a whole command, “go slowly”. kam, “how much, how often”, exclaims; in la-kam it takes la- of emphasis. jāra, “to act unjustly”, and iʿtadā, Form VIII of ʿ-d-w, “to transgress”. rāḥa is to go in the evening, ightadā, Form VIII of gh-d-w, to set out early in the morning; bi- with a verb of going means “taking along”, so Time goes off with his brothers at evening and at dawn, that is, at every hour. mā āna an, “has the time not come that”: āna is “to draw near”, of a time; its twin anā, yaʾnī, is the verb of the Qurʾān's “has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts be humbled” (57:16); the question is not marked, mā being the plain negative, and the asking is in the voice. The print writes āna with a bare alif carrying a dagger alif, اٰنَ, where madda would be usual. rathā li-, “to pity, feel for”: li- marks what is pitied, here “the length of my scattering”; tashattut, Form V of sh-t-t, “being scattered”, is his family and fortune broken up. After an the verb should be subjunctive, tarthiya, but the metre needs a long tarthī, and the poets drop the -ya so; the print spells it with ى, تَرْثِى. turiqqa: the print points the tāʾ with a damma, which makes it Form IV of r-q-q; the usual verb for “to grow tender, relent” is Form I raqqa, yariqqu, which would give tariqqa, the metre being the same; the print's damma is kept. jalmad, “a rock, a great stone”: ka- means “like”; qalbuhu is sung long, qalbuhū, for the metre. In line 3, asāʾa, Form IV of s-w-ʾ, “to do harm to”, takes its object directly; the print sets the hamza's seat as a bare alif with a sukūn and closes the tāʾ with a sukūn too, وَاَسَاْتْ, which would leave the verb without the -a of “you”; the sense and the metre want asaʾta, and the transliteration gives it. The rest of the first half does not construe or scan cleanly. shamita bi- is “to rejoice at someone's misfortune”: bi- marks the victim; ashmata, the Form IV the print has, is “to make someone gloat over”, and wants the gloaters as its object, but the print points kullu al-ʿidāti as the subject. And bi-mā ashmata bī ends the half-line long–short–short–long, a measure kāmil does not have. A likely reading is ashmatta, “you made gloat”, with the tāʾ of the verb and the tāʾ of “you” run together: that scans, and gives Time its verb, though it would want kulla; either way the sense is that Time's doings have set all his enemies gloating. The print is kept. al-radī, “evil”, is radīʾ with its hamza dropped at the rhyme; min sets out what mā covers. ishtafā, Form VIII of sh-f-y, “to be healed”, is used of rancour sated by the sight of the enemy's ruin, as in the poem of the night before. The print writes raʾā without its hamza, رَاى. ghurba, “being a stranger, exile”; ṣabāba, “ardent longing”; tawaḥḥud, Form V of w-ḥ-d, “being alone”. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, as in بِاِخْوَانِي, اَنْ, اَحْبَابِيْ and اَشْمَتَ, and sets a sukūn on the long vowel in تَجُوْرُ, تَرُوْحُ, لِطُوْلِ, اَحْبَابِيْ and الرَّدِيْ, a mark a long vowel does not need.

sentences.t:
لَمْ يَكْفِهِ مَاحَلَّ بِي مِنْ كُرْبَةٍ * وَفِرَاقِ اَحْبَابٍ وَطَرْفٍ اَرْمَدِ
حَتَّى بُلِيتُ بِضِيقِ سِجْنٍ لَيْسَ لِي * فِيهِ اَنِيسٌ غَيْرَ عَضٍّ بِالْيَدِ
وَمَدَامِعٍ تَهْمِي كَفَيْضِ سَحَائِبٍ * وَغَلِيلِ شَوْقٍ نَارُهُ لَمْ تَخْمُدِ
وَكَآبَةٍ وَصَبَابَةٍ وَتَذَكُّرٍ * وَتَحَسُّرٍ وَتَنَفُّسٍ وَتَنَهُّدِ
شَوْقٌ اُكَابِدُهُ وَحُزْنٌ مُتْلِفٌ * وَوَقَعْتُ فِي وَجْدٍ مُقِيمٍ مُقْعِدِ
لَمْ اَلْقَ لِي مِنْ عَاطِفٍ ذِي رَحْمَةٍ * يَحْنُو عَلَيَّ بِزَوْرَةِ الْمُتَرَدِّدِ
هَلْ مِنْ صَدِيقٍ ذِي وِدَادٍ صَادِقٍ * يَرْثٰى لِاَسْقَامِي وَطُولِ تَسَهُّدِي
اَشْكُو اِلَيْهِ مَا اُكَابِدُهُ اَسًى * وَالطَّرْفُ مِنِّي سَاهِرٌ لَمْ يَرْقُدِ
sentences.tr:
lam yakfihi mā ḥalla bī min kurbatin * wa-firāqi aḥbābin wa-ṭarfin armadī
ḥattā bulītu bi-ḍīqi sijnin laysa lī * fīhi anīsun ghayra ʿaḍḍin bi-al-yadī
wa-madāmiʿin tahmī ka-fayḍi saḥāʾibin * wa-ghalīli shawqin nāruhu lam takhmudī
wa-kaʾābatin wa-ṣabābatin wa-tadhakkurin * wa-taḥassurin wa-tanaffusin wa-tanahhudī
shawqun ukābiduhu wa-ḥuznun mutlifun * wa-waqaʿtu fī wajdin muqīmin muqʿidī
lam alqa lī min ʿāṭifin dhī raḥmatin * yaḥnū ʿalayya bi-zawrati al-mutaraddidī
hal min ṣadīqin dhī widādin ṣādiqin * yarthī li-asqāmī wa-ṭūli tasahhudī
ashkū ilayhi mā ukābiduhu asan * wa-al-ṭarfu minnī sāhirun lam yarqudī
sentences.l:
Not sufficed-him what befell me of distress * and-parting-from loved-ones and-an-eye inflamed,
until I-was-afflicted with-(the)-narrowness (of) a-prison; not-is for-me * in-it a-companion other-than a-biting on-the-hand,
and-tear-founts (that) pour like-(the)-overflow (of) clouds, * and-a-burning-thirst (of) longing, its-fire has-not died-down,
and-dejection and-love-longing and-remembering * and-regretting and-sighing and-groaning.
A-longing I-endure-it, and-a-grief destroying; * and-I-have-fallen into a-passion staying, crippling.
Not I-found for-me of a-kindly-one, possessor (of) mercy, * (who) bends over-me with-(the)-visit (of) the-one-who-comes-again-and-again.
Is-there of a-friend, possessor (of) affection true, * (who) pities my-sicknesses and-(the)-length (of) my-sleeplessness,
(that) I-complain to-him (of) what I-endure-it, (in) grief, * while-the-eye of-me (is) wakeful, has-not slept?
sentences.i:
It was not enough for him, all the distress that has come upon me, * the parting from those I love, and eyes inflamed with weeping,
but I must be afflicted with a narrow prison, where I have * no companion but the biting of my hand,
and tears that pour like rain from the clouds, * and the burning thirst of longing whose fire will not die,
and gloom, and yearning, and memory, * and regret, and sighing, and groans.
Longing I endure, and grief that wastes me; * I have fallen into a passion that stays and will not let me rise.
I have found no kindly soul with mercy in him * to bend over me and visit me again and again.
Is there no friend whose love is true, * to pity my sickness and my long nights without sleep,
to whom I might tell the grief I bear, * while my eyes stay open and never sleep?
sentences.n: The middle of the poem. lam yakfihi, “it was not enough for him”: “him” is most naturally the enemy of the line before, whose malice is not yet sated; it may also be Time, now spoken of in the third person. ḥalla bi-, “to alight on, befall”: bi- marks the one it befalls; the print sets mā and ḥalla together as one word, مَاحَلَّ. min sets out what mā covers: distress, parting, and an armad eye, one sore and inflamed, here with weeping. ḥattā bulītu bi-, “until I was afflicted with”: buliya is the passive of balā, “to try, afflict”, and bi- marks the affliction. laysa lī fīhi anīsun, “there is not for me in it a companion”, the Arabic way of saying “I have no companion there”; ghayra, “other than”, is in the accusative of exception. ʿaḍḍ bi-al-yad, “biting on the hand”, is biting one's own hand or fingers, the gesture of remorse and helpless rage; with ʿaḍḍa, “to bite”, bi- marks the thing bitten. Everything that follows, down to the end of line 4 of this part, is in the genitive, still governed by ghayra: “no companion but biting, and tears, and burning, and gloom …”. madāmiʿ, plural of madmaʿ, the place the tears flow from, here the tears themselves; madāmiʿ and saḥāʾib are diptotes in Classical Arabic, without tanwīn, but the print gives both a tanwīn, as the metre needs: a licence the poets allow themselves. hamā, yahmī, “to pour, stream”; ka-, “like”; ghalīl, “the burning of thirst”; khamada, “to die down”, of a fire. The fourth line is a list of six verbal nouns, four of them Form V: tadhakkur, “remembering”, taḥassur, “sighing with regret”, tanaffus, “breathing hard”, tanahhud, “heaving sighs”; kaʾāba is “gloom, dejection”, and its madda, وَكَآبَةٍ, is printed. kābada, Form III of k-b-d, “to endure, struggle with”; mutlif, active participle of Form IV of t-l-f, “that destroys”. wajd, “passion, love-grief”; muqīm, “staying”, and muqʿid, “that keeps one sitting, crippling”, play on standing, qāma, and sitting, qaʿada. lam alqa, “I did not find”, is the jussive of laqiya; min after a negative means “any”. ʿāṭif, “one who inclines, kindly”; ḥanā ʿalā, “to bend over with tenderness”: ʿalā marks the one cared for. bi-zawrati al-mutaraddid, “with the visit of one who keeps coming”: bi- marks the manner; al-mutaraddid, Form V of r-d-d, “one who comes and goes, again and again”. hal min ṣadīqin, “is there any friend”: min after hal also means “any”. widād, “love, affection”. The print points the verb of line 7 with a dagger alif on its thāʾ, يَرْثٰى, which would make it yarthā; the verb is rathā, yarthī, as the print itself has it in tarthī, and it is read yarthī here, the printed mark kept in the Arabic; the metre is the same either way. li- again marks what is pitied. shakā ilā, “to complain to”: ilā marks the one complained to. asan, “grief”, is an accusative, “out of grief”. In lines 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 the pronoun -hi or -hu is sung long for the metre, yakfihī, fīhī, nāruhū, ukābiduhū, ilayhī, as the poets regularly do. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, as in اَحْبَابٍ, اَرْمَدِ, اَنِيسٌ, اُكَابِدُهُ, اَلْقَ, لِاَسْقَامِي, اَشْكُو, اِلَيْهِ and اَسًى; the ئ of سَحَائِبٍ is printed.

sentences.t:
وَيَطُولُ لَيْلِي فِى الْعَذَابِ لِاَنَّنِي * اَصْلِي بِنَارِ الْهَمِّ ذَاتِ تَوَقُّدِ
اَلْبَقُّ وَالْبَرْغُوْثُ قَدْ شَرِبَا دَمِي * شُرْبَ الطِّلَا مِنْ كَفِّ اَلْمَى اَغْيَدِ
وَالْجِسْمُ بَيْنَ الْقَمْلِ مِنِّي قَدْ حَكَى * مَالَ الْيَتِيمِ بِكَفِّ قَاضٍ مُلْحِدِ
وَسَكَنْتُ فِى قَبْرٍ ثَلٰثَةِ اَذْرُعٍ * وَغَدَوْتُ بَيْنَ مُقَيَّدٍ وَمُفَصَّدِ
فَمُدَامَتِي دَمْعِي وَقَيْدِي مُطْرِبِي * وَالْفِكْرُ نُقْلِي وَالْهُمُومُ تَمَهُّدِي
sentences.tr:
wa-yaṭūlu laylī fī al-ʿadhābi li-annanī * aṣlī bi-nāri al-hammi dhāti tawaqqudī
al-baqqu wa-al-barghūthu qad sharibā damī * shurba al-ṭilā min kaffi almā aghyadī
wa-al-jismu bayna al-qamli minnī qad ḥakā * māla al-yatīmi bi-kaffi qāḍin mulḥidī
wa-sakantu fī qabrin thalāthati adhruʿin * wa-ghadawtu bayna muqayyadin wa-mufaṣṣadī
fa-mudāmatī damʿī wa-qaydī muṭribī * wa-al-fikru nuqlī wa-al-humūmu tamahhudī
sentences.l:
And-grows-long my-night in the-torment, because-I * burn in-(the)-fire (of) the-care, possessor (of) blazing.
The-bugs and-the-flea have drunk my-blood, * (the) drinking (of) the-wine from (the) palm (of) a-dark-lipped-one, supple-necked.
And-the-body among the-lice, of-me, has resembled * (the) property (of) the-orphan in-(the)-palm (of) a-judge godless.
And-I-have-dwelt in a-grave (of) three cubits, * and-I-have-become between fettered and-bled.
So-my-wine (is) my-tears, and-my-fetter my-music-maker, * and-the-thought my-wine-sweets, and-the-cares my-bedding.
sentences.i:
My night is long in torment, for I * am burning in the fire of care, and it blazes.
The bugs and the flea have drunk my blood * as wine is drunk from the hand of a supple youth with dusky lips.
My body among the lice has fared * like an orphan's wealth in the hands of a godless judge.
I dwell in a grave three cubits long, * and I live between my fetters and my bleeding.
My wine is my tears, my fetter my minstrel, * my thoughts the sweetmeats to my wine, and my cares my bed.
sentences.n: The last five lines turn the prison into a drinking-party, the setting of the wine-song: the vermin drink his blood as wine is drunk from a cupbearer's hand, and in the closing line his tears are his wine, his fetter his musician, his thoughts the nuql, the dried fruit and sweets nibbled with wine, and his cares his bed. li-annanī, “because I”: li- of cause with anna and the “I” suffix. For “to burn in, be roasted in” a fire, the Classical verb is ṣaliya, yaṣlā; aṣlī belongs to ṣalā, yaṣlī, “to roast” something, but the sense is plain, and bi- marks the fire he burns in. dhāti tawaqqud, “possessed of blazing”: dhāt is feminine, agreeing with nār, “fire”; tawaqqud, Form V of w-q-d. al-baqq, “bugs”, is a collective and al-barghūth, “the flea”, a singular standing for the kind, and the verb is dual, sharibā, for the two of them; the print sets a fatḥa on the alif of the article in اَلْبَقُّ, as it does at the head of a line. shurba al-ṭilā, “the drinking of ṭilāʾ”, a verbal noun of comparison, “as one drinks”: ṭilāʾ, wine boiled down thick, here without its hamza. اَلْمَى is not the article: it is almā, of the pattern afʿal from l-m-y, “dark-lipped”, the dusky red of the lips that the poets admired; aghyad, “soft and swaying in the neck”: both describe the beautiful cupbearer. As afʿal adjectives both are diptotes, and aghyad would properly have -a in the genitive; the kasra is the rhyme's. ḥakā, “to resemble”: his body among the lice is like an orphan's property in the keeping of a corrupt judge, eaten away bit by bit. The qāḍī had charge of the estates of orphans, and the judge who devours them is a stock figure of satire; mulḥid, “one who swerves from the faith, godless”. qabrin thalāthati adhruʿin, “a grave of three cubits”: the number phrase stands beside qabr in the genitive and describes it; the dagger alif of ثَلٰثَةِ is printed. ghadā, first “to go out in the morning”, is used as “to become”, like ṣāra. mufaṣṣad, passive participle of Form II of f-ṣ-d, “bled, with the veins opened”: the beatings have let his blood. mudāma, “wine”, so called because it is kept long in the jar; muṭrib, “one who moves to delight”, a musician or singer: the clank of the fetter is his music. tamahhud, Form V of m-h-d, “being smoothed out, laid as a bed”: his cares are what he lies on. The word looks like a slip for tanahhud, “groaning”, but tanahhud has already served as the rhyme of line 8 of the poem, and the printed word fits the picture of the feast; it is kept. fī is spelled with ى, فِى, in lines 1 and 4, and the print sets a sukūn on the long vowel in الْبَرْغُوْثُ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَنَظْمِهِ وَنَثْرِهِ أَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَتَذَكَّرَ مَاكَانَ فِيهِ وَمَا حَصَلَ لَهُ مِنْ فِرَاقِ أَخِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi wa-naẓmihi wa-nathrihi anna wa-ishtakā wa-tadhakkara mā kāna fīhi wa-mā ḥaṣala lahu min firāqi akhīhi
sentences.l: And-when he-finished from his-verse and-his-stringing and-his-scattering, he-moaned and-complained, and-remembered what he-was in-it and-what happened to-him of (the) parting-from his-brother.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, his rhymes and his prose, he moaned and lamented, and thought of the state he had once been in, and of all that had come to him from the parting from his brother.
sentences.n: shiʿr, naẓm and nathr, “verse, composition and prose”, is a storyteller's jingle: he has spoken no prose, and the three words simply round off “when he had finished reciting”. naẓm, “stringing” pearls, is the making of verse; nathr, “scattering”, is prose. faragha min, “to finish with”: min marks what is done. ḥaṣala li-, “to come about for, befall”: li- marks the one it befalls; min sets out what mā covers. firāqu akhīhi, “the parting from his brother”: the genitive marks the one parted from. The print sets mā and kāna as one word, ماكان, here and twice more below, and that is kept. The shadda of انّ and of تذكّر is printed.

The storyteller's formula for leaving one character and turning to another: “this is what there was of his affair”. It is answered at once by wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “and as for what there was of the affair of …”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ أَخِيهِ الْأَمْجَدِ فَإِنَّهُ مَكَثَ يَنْتَظِرُ أَخَاهُ الْأَسْعَدَ إِلَى نِصْفِ النَّهَارِ فَمَا عَادَ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri akhīhi al-Amjadi fa-innahu makatha yantaẓiru akhāhu al-Asʿada ilā niṣfi al-nahāri fa-mā ʿāda ilayhi
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) his-brother al-Amjad, then-indeed-he stayed waiting-for his-brother al-Asʿad until (the) half (of) the-day, and-not he-returned to-him.
sentences.i: As for his brother al-Amjad, he waited for al-Asʿad until midday, and his brother did not come back to him.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … then”: whatever answers ammā must open with fa-, here fa-innahu. makatha, “to stay, remain”, with an imperfect after it, yantaẓiru, “waiting”: the imperfect says what he was doing while he stayed. niṣf al-nahār, “the half of the day”, is noon. fa-mā ʿāda, “and he did not return”: mā with a past verb is the plain negative of the past.

sentences.t: فَخَفَقَ فُؤَادُهُ وَاشْتَدَّ بِهِ أَلَمُ الْفِرَاقِ وَأَفَاضَ دَمْعَهُ الْمُهْرَاقَ
sentences.tr: fa-khafaqa fuʾāduhu wa-ishtadda bihi alamu al-firāqi wa-afāḍa damʿahu al-muhrāqa
sentences.l: And-throbbed his-heart, and-grew-hard on-him (the) pain (of) the-parting, and-he-made-overflow his-tears, the-poured-out.
sentences.i: His heart began to pound, the pain of parting pressed hard upon him, and he let his tears pour freely.
sentences.n: khafaqa, “to beat, flutter”, of the heart in fear. fuʾād, “heart”: the hamza of فؤاده is printed. ishtadda bihi, Form VIII of sh-d-d, “to grow severe upon him”: bi- marks the one it weighs on; the shadda of واشتدّ is printed. afāḍa, Form IV of f-y-ḍ, “to make overflow, pour forth”. damʿ, “tears”, a collective. al-muhrāq, “poured out”, passive participle of ahrāqa, an old by-form of arāqa, “to pour”, with h in place of hamza; the epithet adds little but the rhyme. The sajʿ falls on al-firāq / al-muhrāq.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print splits the name here, شهر زاد; it is kept as set.
